title: Episode 30: The Great Fire of 1910 and Ed Pulaski's Mine Tunnel
description:
In August 1910, hurricane-force gale winds whipped hundreds of small forest fires in northern Idaho and western Montana into a colossal firestorm known as the 'Big Blowup.' Burning three million acres of virgin white pine in thirty-six hours, the fire threatened to incinerate the crew of veteran ranger Edward Pulaski, who forced forty panicked firefighters into an abandoned prospecting tunnel and held them at gunpoint with wet blankets to save their lives.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the hot, parched summer of nineteen ten, the northern Rockies were a tinderbox waiting for a spark. Following months of severe drought, lightning strikes ignited thousands of small blazes across northern Idaho and Montana. On August twentieth, hurricane-force winds of seventy miles per hour roared through the Bitterroot Mountains, merging the blazes into an apocalyptic firestorm that incinerated three million acres in just thirty-six hours. Trapped in a wall of roaring flame, veteran Forest Service ranger Edward Pulaski made a fateful decision that saved forty lives and forged an enduring American legend. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE SUMMER OF SMOKE
The summer of nineteen ten in the Pacific Northwest was the driest in recorded meteorological history. By mid-July, no measurable rain had fallen across the dense river basins of northern Idaho or western Montana for more than ten consecutive weeks. The dense, ancient forests of western white pine, Douglas fir, and cedar—some trees soaring over two hundred feet tall and centuries old—were bone dry and as explosive as sawdust soaked in gasoline. Across the Bitterroot Range, hundreds of small fires were ignited by glowing cinders from coal-burning steam locomotive smokestacks, careless prospectors, and violent dry lightning storms. The United States Forest Service was an infant agency barely five years old, created by President Theodore Roosevelt and Chief Forester Gifford Pinchot to protect the public domain against ruthless timber monopolies. The agency had virtually no specialized firefighting equipment, relying on two-man crosscut saws, round-point shovels, and double-bit axes, and possessing only a handful of permanent rangers scattered across millions of acres of roadless wilderness. To combat the spreading flames, rangers recruited thousands of temporary laborers from Spokane skid rows, lumber camps, and mining towns, alongside regular federal troops dispatched by President William Howard Taft. Among the most respected veteran rangers on the Coeur d'Alene National Forest was Edward Pulaski, a forty-two-year-old former prospector, engineer, and blacksmith who knew every canyon and ridge of the Bitterroot Mountains like the back of his hand.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE BIG BLOWUP ARRIVES
On the afternoon of Saturday, August twentieth, nineteen ten, disaster struck with unimaginable, cosmic fury. A ferocious dry cold front swept in from the Pacific Northwest, bringing sustained gale-force winds of seventy miles per hour that howled through the narrow mountain passes. Within hours, the howling winds whipped more than three thousand separate small fires into a single, colossal wall of roaring flame known forever in frontier history as the 'Big Blowup.' The firestorm behaved like an inland hurricane of fire: it created its own terrifying atmospheric system, generating superheated convective vortexes that ripped giant centuries-old trees out of the ground by their roots and hurled flaming logs across entire valleys like burning spears. The roar of the firestorm was deafening, sounding like the simultaneous bombardment of a thousand naval cannons, and could be heard in Missoula, Montana, more than one hundred miles away. Darkness fell at mid-day as a colossal pyrocumulus cloud of black smoke rose forty thousand feet into the stratosphere, blocking out the sun and turning noon into midnight across four states and western Canada. In Wallace, Idaho, a prosperous mining town nestled in a narrow canyon, alarm bells clanged as fire leaped across the bluffs, forcing thousands of women and children onto evacuation trains just minutes before the wooden trestle bridges burned behind them.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: TRAPPED IN THE PLACER CREEK CANYON
Five miles south of Wallace, Ranger Ed Pulaski was in command of a crew of forty-five weary, soot-covered firefighters battling the flames along the high ridge dividing the Coeur d'Alene and St. Joe rivers. As the hurricane winds roared through the canopy, Pulaski realized with sickening clarity that the fire had crowned—leaping into the tops of the white pines and racing toward them through the treetops at thirty miles an hour. Their escape route back to Wallace was completely severed by a towering wall of flame three hundred feet high that roared up the gulch. Panicked men began screaming, throwing down their axes and shovels, and attempting to run blindly down the burning canyon, where they would have been incinerated within seconds. Pulaski, keeping an iron composure amidst the deafening tempest, knew that outrunning the crown fire was physically impossible. He remembered an old, abandoned prospecting tunnel called the Nicholson adit, driven into the cold granite bluff near Placer Creek. Shouting over the deafening roar of the flames, Pulaski commanded his men to drop their heavy packframes, seize their woolen blankets, and follow him through the suffocating smoke. Two men broke away in terror and vanished into the inferno; Pulaski led the remaining forty-two men and their pack horses in a desperate race against the flaming shockwave.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE NICHOLSON ADIT AT GUNPOINT
They reached the mouth of the Nicholson adit just as the fire swept over the canyon. The tunnel was a narrow horizontal drift, six feet high and barely seven feet wide, cutting one hundred feet straight into the cold granite hillside. Pulaski herded forty-two terrified men and their horses into the dark cavern. Inside, conditions rapidly deteriorated into a living nightmare. The firestorm roared past the entrance like a blowtorch, instantly consuming the wooden tunnel timbers and sucking all the oxygen from the air. Pulaski snatched wet woolen horse blankets from the stream bed, hanging them across the tunnel mouth to block out the searing radiant heat. Still, thick clouds of blinding smoke and suffocating carbon monoxide billowed into the cavern. Terrified that the tunnel would become a tomb, one panicked laborer screamed: 'We're all going to burn! I'm getting out!' and made a lunge toward the flaming opening. Pulaski drew his forty-five caliber revolver, leveled it squarely at the man's chest, and shouted above the roar: 'The first man who tries to leave this tunnel, I will shoot him dead. Lie down on the floor and cover your faces!' Every man obeyed, throwing himself face down into the cold mud and trickle of water on the tunnel floor, where the last scraps of breathable air remained.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE ORDEAL IN THE MUD
For five agonizing hours, Pulaski stood sentinel at the entrance of the burning tunnel. While his men lay in the mud weeping, praying, and gasping for breath, Pulaski repeatedly soaked blankets in the muddy pool and threw them against the burning entrance timbers. His clothes caught fire; his hands were seared down to the bone, and his face and eyes were severely blistered by the intense thermal radiation. Still, he refused to abandon his post. Around midnight, the horses suffocated, collapsing onto the tunnel floor, and five men near the front succumbed to carbon monoxide poisoning and died. Finally, overcome by smoke and toxic fumes, Pulaski himself collapsed unconscious face down in the mud. Hours later, at dawn on August twenty-first, the firestorm subsided, leaving behind a smoking, smoldering wasteland of blackened stumps and white ash. One surviving firefighter stirred in the darkness, crawled to the entrance, and looked down at Pulaski's motionless, blistered body. The man whispered: 'The boss is dead.' Hearing the voice, Pulaski groaned from the mud: 'Like hell I am. Get up and get into town.' Blinded and in excruciating agony, Pulaski stood up, and thirty-seven surviving men walked out of the granite tunnel into the daylight.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE INVENTION OF THE PULASKI TOOL
The Big Blowup of nineteen ten burned over three million acres of timber, destroyed one-third of the city of Wallace, and claimed the lives of eighty-five people, seventy-eight of them firefighters. It remains the largest wildfire in American history. Ed Pulaski spent weeks in the Wallace hospital recovering from his burns and remained partially blind and afflicted with respiratory damage for the rest of his life. Yet he refused to abandon his beloved mountains, returning to his duties as a Forest Service ranger in Wallace. Haunting memories of his men's desperate struggle drove Pulaski to improve wildland firefighting technology. Working in his home blacksmith shop during the winter of nineteen eleven, Pulaski forged a revolutionary dual-purpose tool designed specifically for battling forest fires. He welded the cutting blade of an axe together with a curved trenching adze onto a single high-carbon steel head fitted with a sturdy hickory handle. This ingenious design allowed a single firefighter to chop heavy roots and scrape firebreaks through mineral soil without switching tools. By nineteen twenty, the Forest Service adopted the design, officially christening it the 'Pulaski.' Today, more than a century later, the Pulaski remains the indispensable standard hand tool carried by every wildland firefighter across North America and around the world.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LEGACY OF GIFFORD PINCHOT'S RANGERS
The catastrophe of nineteen ten profoundly reshaped American conservation and federal land policy. Prior to the firestorm, critics in Congress had derided the Forest Service as an expensive, unnecessary bureaucratic invention, repeatedly threatening to defund the agency and sell public forests to private timber syndicates. But the heroic sacrifice of rangers like Ed Pulaski galvanized public support nationwide. Former Chief Forester Gifford Pinchot and President William Howard Taft used the tragedy to secure the landmark Weeks Act of nineteen eleven, which granted the federal government authority to purchase and protect private watershed lands, expanding the national forest system across the eastern United States. Furthermore, the disaster established the Forest Service's aggressive policy of total fire suppression, which governed American forest management for the next six decades. Today, the Nicholson adit in Placer Creek Canyon is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Visitors hike along the Pulaski Tunnel Trail beneath towering second-growth pines, arriving at the mouth of the granite cavern where forty men faced down an ocean of fire, preserved forever as a monument to frontier courage, grit, and the birth of modern conservation.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Great Fire of 1910 and Ed Pulaski's stand in the mountain tunnel remind us of the extraordinary sacrifices made by wildland firefighters who protect our natural heritage. It shows that true leadership is tested not in calm waters, but in the heart of the storm. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we explore Idaho's legendary sheep wars and the gunslinger who would not hang. Until then, stay curious.
